newsitem.title: USA: Calm returns to riot-torn Florida city.
newsitem.headline: Calm returns to riot-torn Florida city.

text.p: An uneasy calm returned to the streets of St. Petersburg on Friday morning after a night of rioting in a mainly-black inner-city neighbourhood sparked by police shooting dead a black motorist.

Hundreds of police, some in riot gear, were still patrolling a large section of the city at 5 a.m. EDT (0900 GMT), but the streets were said to have been cleared of rioters and the situation brought under control.

Twenty people were arrested as angry gangs of youths rampaged through the city, throwing rocks, bricks and bottles at police and setting fire to cars and businesses. Police estimated the number of rioters were "in the hundreds".

At least 11 people were injured. Six police officers, one firefighter and four journalists were treated for cuts and minor injuries and later released from hospital, said police spokeswoman Lilla Davis.
She said that during the night as many as 500 police officers were deployed in the city to quell rioting and that by 3.30 a.m. EDT (0730 GMT) the situation was under control.
"It is all calm now and has been for the last two hours," she said at 5.30 a.m. (0930 GMT). "It was still tense until about 3.30.
"Police, some in riot gear, remain on the streets to keep the situation under control. It is getting quieter all the time," Davis told Reuters.

During the disturbances, which began about 7:30 p.m. EDT on Thursday (1130 GMT) and stretched across a large area bounded by 16th and 34th streets and 5th Avenue to 62nd Avenue, a series of fires were lit by the rioters, said Davis.

Firefighters were unable to reach some of the burning buildings, advancing slowly down the street toward burning houses under guard by a line of police. All fires were now been extinguished, said Davis.

St. Petersburg Mayor David Fisher said the state attorney's office would investigate the shooting incident. City officials will meet with black community leaders on Friday morning to try to prevent a recurrence of violence.
"These things are spontaneous, it just ignites," said Fisher. "It's a wake-up call that you have a lot of work to do."
Police said the incident began when two officers, a white male and a white female, stopped a car for speeding in a south St. Petersburg neighbourhood with a history of trouble with drug dealers.

They shot the motorist because they believed he was trying to run them down after his gold Pontiac lurched forward, police said. But some witnesses said the driver had done nothing to prompt the shooting.
"She shot him for nothing, nothing," Rachel Wilson, who witnessed the traffic stop, told St. Petersburg television station WTOG.
Wilson said the car's driver had his hands in the air when he was shot. The man died before reaching Bayfront Medical Centre, a local hospital.

The riot began shortly afterward at the intersection where the shooting took place. The crowd began to throw rocks and bottles at police, and scattered rioting quickly spread over several blocks as word of the shooting spread.
Community leaders called for calm and attributed the violence to small groups of young men who were roaming the streets setting fires, looting and throwing bricks and rocks.
